title: Design and Execute AI Security Testing and Red Teaming
intro: Testing AI systems the way attackers and real users will: scoping assessments around the whole system, with objectives, scenarios, success criteria and rules of engagement; running safe adversarial tests against generative AI, RAG and agentic architectures; applying red teaming methodologies that combine human creativity with automation; and using AI-assisted tools to evaluate controls and discover new attack paths.
objectives: Scope AI security assessments with objectives, scenarios, measurable success criteria and signed rules of engagement
Design safe adversarial tests for GenAI, RAG and agentic architectures, and measure results as attack success rates
Apply AI red teaming methodologies and frameworks, combining human-led and automated testing in break-fix cycles
Use AI-assisted tools to evaluate AI controls and find novel attack paths, with safeguards for scope, judging and data
Explain the root causes and families of jailbreaks and injection, and measure resistance with attack success and false refusal rates

scenes.title: Planning an AI security assessment
scenes.say: An AI security test is only as good as its plan. Test the wrong thing, in the wrong environment, without clear objectives, and you get a pile of interesting outputs and no answers. | This video covers how to scope AI security assessments, set objectives, and design test scenarios that tell you something real.

scenes.title: Test the system, not just the model
scenes.say: Scope the whole system, not just the model, because most real failures happen where components meet. | The model: its behaviour, its refusals, and any leakage of training or system data. | The application: system prompts, guardrails, and how outputs are handled downstream. | Data and retrieval: sources, indexes, and whether retrieval respects permissions. | Agents and tools: scopes, approval steps and memory. | Infrastructure: serving endpoints, pipelines and keys, where traditional testing still applies. | And people and process: whether human reviewers, monitoring and incident response catch what gets through.

scenes.title: From threat model to test plan

nodes.label: Objectives
nodes.sub: impacts to prove or rule out

scenes.say: Good scenarios come from the threat model, built as Module 6.1 described: who might attack, what they want, and how they could get in. | Turn that into objectives: the impacts you want to prove or rule out, such as leaking customer data or triggering an unauthorised refund. | Each objective becomes one or more scenarios, naming an actor, an entry point, a class of technique and a target. | Define success criteria in advance, such as the highest acceptable attack success rate for each category. | Agree rules of engagement: who authorised the test, what is in scope, and the limits testers must respect. | Then write the test plan: the cases, how many times each will be repeated, and the schedule.

scenes.title: Choosing the assessment type
scenes.say: Choose the assessment type that fits the question. | Automated evaluations measure known risks at scale. A penetration test looks for exploitable flaws within a defined scope. A red team exercise pursues a real adversary’s goals, wherever they lead within the rules. | Automated evaluations run suites and benchmarks on every release. Penetration tests are systematic and time-boxed. Red teams are creative, objective-led and end to end. | Automated evaluations produce scores and trends. Penetration tests produce findings with severities. Red teams produce attack paths, and show where detection and response failed. Mature programmes use all three.

blocks.md:
### Scoping an AI security assessment
- **System, not model:** include the application, retrieval pipeline, agents and tools, infrastructure, and the human processes around them. Many serious findings sit at the joins, such as retrieved content reaching a tool call (Module 4.1).
- **Assets and entry points:** list what must be protected (data, credentials, actions, safety properties) and every way content gets in: user input, files, retrieved documents, tool outputs, memory and other agents.
- **Third parties:** hosted models, tools and connectors have their own terms. Check that the provider allows security testing, use its testing or bug bounty route where one exists, and never test another organisation’s systems without permission (Module 6.3).
- **Environment:** test in a staging environment that matches production (the same model version, prompts, guardrails, tools and permissions) but holds **synthetic or canary data**. Test in production only with explicit approval and tight limits.

### Objectives and scenarios
Objectives state the impacts to prove or rule out, derived from the threat model (Module 6.1):
| Category | Example objective |
|---|---|
| **Confidentiality** | Can a user retrieve another customer’s records, or the system prompt? |
| **Integrity** | Can planted content change answers or decisions? |
| **Agency** | Can the agent be steered into an action it isn’t authorised to take? |
| **Availability and cost** | Can inputs drive runaway loops or token consumption? |
| **Safety and misuse** | Can safeguards against harmful output be bypassed? |

Each **scenario** names an actor (an external user, an insider, a poisoned data source or a compromised tool), an entry point, a technique class such as indirect prompt injection, a target, and the evidence that proves success. Draw technique classes from the **OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications**, the **OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications**, **MITRE ATLAS** and your own incident history, and track them in a **coverage matrix**.

### Designing tests for stochastic systems
- **Repeat each case** many times at production settings, because the same input can succeed on one attempt and fail on the next. Report an **attack success rate** (Module 1.3), not a single pass or fail.
- **Pin and record versions** of the model, prompts, guardrails and tools, so results can be compared and reproduced (Module 6.5).
- **Include multi-turn and multimodal cases:** many attacks build up over a conversation, or hide in images, audio and documents.
- **Set success criteria in advance**, such as a maximum attack success rate for high-severity categories, so results lead to decisions.

### Assessment types and knowledge levels
| Type | Best for |
|---|---|
| **Automated evaluation** | Known risks, at scale, on every release (Module 6.6) |
| **Penetration test** | Exploitable flaws in a defined scope and time box |
| **Red team exercise** | Realistic adversary objectives end to end, including whether detection and response work |
| **Bug bounty** | Continuous, diverse external testing, once the basics are in place |

Testers may get no internal knowledge (**black box**), some, such as the architecture and system prompts (**grey box**), or full access, including code and weights (**white box**). More knowledge finds more in the time available.

### Rules of engagement
Signed authorisation from risk owners; scope and exclusions; objectives; methods; limits such as canary data only and rate caps; **stop rules** for real data exposure or harm; testing windows; communication and escalation paths; handling of harmful outputs and tester wellbeing; and reporting timelines.

blocks.title: The production shortcut
blocks.md: A team plans to red team its new claims-handling agent before launch. To save time, the team lead proposes testing directly in production, using real claims data and without written approval, because “staging doesn’t have the latest prompts”.

q.q: What should the security lead require FIRST?
o: Testing in production, with testers asked to take care with any real claims data they see
Signed rules of engagement, and a production-matching staging environment with canary data
Cancelling the red team, since agents can’t be tested safely while their prompts keep changing
Testing in production overnight, when fewer customers are likely to be affected by problems
q.why: Testing needs written authorisation, a clear scope and limits, and an environment that matches production without exposing real data. Bringing staging up to date with the latest prompts fixes the stated problem. Asking for care, cancelling or testing overnight doesn’t address authorisation or data exposure.

blocks.title: Scoping questions
blocks.md: Strong answers **scope the whole system**, derive **objectives and scenarios from the threat model**, set **measurable success criteria**, and run tests under **signed rules of engagement** in a **production-like environment with canary data**. Remember that AI is stochastic: one passing attempt proves little, so **repeat tests and report rates**.

q.q: A red team runs each prompt injection test case once and reports that the assistant "passed". Why is this result unreliable?
o: Prompt injection tests are only valid when external testers run them
Outputs vary between attempts, so cases need repeating to estimate a rate
Single tests are fine, provided they are run at weekends to avoid traffic
The assistant should have been tested by the developers who built it
q.why: The same input can succeed on one attempt and fail on another. Repeating each case at production settings gives an attack success rate, which is the meaningful measure.

sections.title: Adversarial testing for GenAI, RAG and agents

scenes.title: Testing where attacks really land
scenes.sub: Adversarial testing for GenAI, RAG and agentic AI
scenes.say: Attacks on AI systems don’t only arrive through the chat box. They arrive in documents, web pages, tool results, memories and messages from other agents. | This video covers adversarial testing for generative AI applications, retrieval-augmented generation and agentic architectures: what to test, and how to test safely.

scenes.title: What to test, by architecture
scenes.say: What you test depends on the architecture. | For a generative AI application, the entry points are prompts, files and images. RAG adds documents, web pages and index content. Agents add tool results, memory and messages from other agents. | Test a GenAI application for jailbreaks, leakage of system prompts or data, and unsafe output. Test RAG for indirect injection, poisoning, and retrieval that bypasses access controls. Test agents for tool misuse, privilege escalation and goal hijacking. | And collect the right evidence: responses and refusals; the chunks that were retrieved and cited; and every tool call, action and trace.

scenes.title: A canary test for indirect injection

msgs.t: Summarise the supplier invoices received this week.
Invoice 4471 · Total £1,240 · [planted test text: a hidden instruction to call the canary tool]
This week: 12 invoices, £18,930 in total. Two are due on Friday.
Result: FAIL. The agent obeyed an instruction found in data.

notes.d: The tester asks for a routine summary, in staging.
Test text asks the agent to call a canary tool.
The tool does nothing except record that it was called.
The summary is normal, so a user would never notice.
No money, data or messages moved.

scenes.say: Here is a safe way to test for indirect injection. In staging, the tester asks a finance assistant to summarise this week’s supplier invoices. | One invoice is a planted test document, containing a hidden instruction to call a canary tool: a tool that does nothing except record that it was called. | The canary fires. The agent has treated text inside a document as an instruction. | Its summary looks perfectly normal, which is exactly why the canary matters: a user would never notice. | The test fails, and it proves the weakness without moving any money, data or messages. The same approach works with canary records, links and tokens.

scenes.title: Test cases for RAG and agents

items.d: Can one user retrieve another’s files?
Can the agent exceed its permissions?
Can it act without required sign-off?
Can it burn tokens and calls?

scenes.say: Six test cases matter especially for RAG and agents. | Permission-aware retrieval: can one user’s question pull back documents they aren’t allowed to see? | Poisoned content: does planted content in the index change answers or recommendations? | Tool and scope limits: can the agent be steered into calls beyond its permissions? | Approval bypass: can it complete a high-impact action without the human approval it should require? | Memory persistence: does an injected instruction survive into later sessions, or into other users’ sessions? | And runaway loops: can inputs drive it into endless tool calls, burning tokens and money?

scenes.def: At a million requests a day, a 2% success rate means 20,000 successful attacks.
scenes.ex: Repeat each case many times, and report the rate, with versions and settings.
scenes.say: One number explains why AI testing is statistical. Imagine an attack that succeeds only two per cent of the time. | At a million requests a day, that is twenty thousand successful attacks, yet a single test run would probably have reported a pass. | So repeat each case many times, at production settings, and report the success rate, together with the model version and settings used.

items: Test every entry point: prompts, documents, tools, memory, agents
Use canaries to prove weaknesses without real harm
Test retrieval permissions, approvals, scopes and loops
Repeat cases, and report attack success rates
scenes.say: To recap. | Test every entry point: prompts, documents, tool results, memory and other agents. | Use canary tools, records and links to prove weaknesses without real harm. | Test retrieval permissions, approval steps, tool scopes and runaway loops. | And repeat cases, reporting attack success rates rather than single results.

blocks.md:
### Test objectives by architecture
| Architecture | Technique classes to test | What good looks like |
|---|---|---|
| **GenAI applications** | Direct prompt injection and jailbreak families (role-play, obfuscation and encoding, multi-turn escalation, many-shot patterns); system prompt and data leakage; unsafe output; improper output handling where output reaches browsers, databases or code (Module 3.5) | Safeguards hold across repeated, multi-turn and multimodal attempts; outputs are treated as untrusted downstream |
| **RAG systems** | Indirect injection through documents and pages; corpus and index poisoning; retrieval that ignores document permissions; leakage between tenants; citation manipulation | Retrieved text is treated as data; retrieval enforces the user’s permissions; poisoned content is detected or contained |
| **Agentic systems** | Tool misuse and excessive agency; confused-deputy actions; approval bypass; memory poisoning; tool poisoning through tool descriptions (Module 4.1); injection between agents; cascading failures; resource exhaustion | Least-privilege tools; approvals that can’t be skipped; memory that doesn’t carry instructions; every action traceable |
| **Multimodal inputs** | Instructions hidden in images, audio, video or file metadata | The same protections apply to every modality |

### Testing safely
- Use **canaries**: tools, records, links or tokens that only record that they were triggered. They prove an instruction was followed without moving money, data or messages.
- Keep tests in **isolated environments** with synthetic data, and never use real exfiltration routes.
- Describe attack content with **neutral placeholders** in shared reports; store harmful outputs securely, on a need-to-know basis.
- Watch for **side effects**: injected content in shared indexes or memory can affect other testers and users, so reset state after each run.

### Measuring results
- **Attack success rate (ASR)** for each technique class, with the number of attempts, model version, settings and guardrail configuration.
- **Turns needed:** how many conversation turns a multi-turn attack required.
- **Detection:** whether monitoring flagged the attempt (Module 5.3), not just whether the attack worked.
- **Benign baselines:** false refusals on legitimate requests, so that fixes don’t break the product.

Public benchmarks help with coverage and comparison: **AgentDojo** for prompt injection against tool-using agents, **HarmBench** for harmful behaviours under automated attack, and **CyberSecEval** for cyber security risks in models. They complement, but never replace, tests of your own system with your own data and tools.

blocks.title: Which test is this?
pairs: Checking whether one user’s question can surface another user’s files
Permission-aware retrieval test
Planting a document that asks the agent to call a canary tool
Indirect injection test
Checking whether a refund can be issued without manager sign-off
Approval bypass test
Hiding an instruction in an image’s pixels or metadata
Multimodal injection test
Seeing whether an injected instruction persists into tomorrow’s session
Memory persistence test

blocks.title: Adversarial testing questions
blocks.md: Match tests to the **architecture’s entry points**: prompts for GenAI; documents and indexes for RAG; tools, memory and other agents for agentic systems. Prefer **safe proofs** such as **canary tools and records** in isolated environments over real exploitation, measure **attack success rates** over repeated attempts, and check **detection** as well as prevention.

q.q: Testers plant a document in a staging index that asks an agent to call a monitored canary tool. Why is this approach preferred?
o: It lets testers move real funds safely, because the canary tool can reverse payments
It proves the agent obeys instructions found in data, without causing any real harm
It removes the need to test the agent’s tools or permissions at any later stage
It guarantees that the agent will never follow hidden instructions in production
q.why: A canary tool only records that it was called, so it shows that the agent followed an instruction embedded in data, with no real-world effect. It doesn’t replace other tests or guarantee future behaviour.

scenes.title: Thinking like an adversary
scenes.say: Red teaming means emulating a real adversary, with their goals and creativity, to find out how a system fails before someone else does. For AI, it also means emulating ordinary users who stumble into harm. | This video covers AI red teaming methodologies: the process, the frameworks, and how to combine human and automated testing.

scenes.title: The AI red team cycle
scenes.intro: Each engagement runs through six stages.
scenes.say: An AI red team engagement runs through six stages. | Plan: agree objectives, scope and rules of engagement. | Map: understand the architecture, data flows and threat model, including every place untrusted content gets in. | Attack: explore manually first, to find promising weaknesses, then scale up with automation. | Assess: verify each finding, score its severity, and make sure it can be reproduced. | Report: describe the findings, the attack paths, and where detection failed. | Fix and retest: the builders mitigate, and the red team tests again. This break-fix cycle repeats, because AI security is never finished.

scenes.title: Human and automated red teaming
scenes.say: Human and automated red teaming complement each other. | Humans bring creativity, context and judgement, including subject expertise and cultural knowledge. Automation brings scale, coverage and repeatability, which matters because AI outputs vary. | Human testing is slow, costly and hard to repeat exactly. Automation misses novel and contextual harms it wasn’t designed to look for. | So use people for new features and high-risk scenarios, and automation for variants, regressions and every release. Microsoft’s AI red team, after testing more than a hundred generative AI products, reached the same conclusion: automation extends coverage, but humans remain essential.

scenes.title: Frameworks that structure the work

items.h: CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide

scenes.say: Several frameworks help structure AI red teaming. | The OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide, from January 2025, covers four areas: model evaluation, implementation testing, infrastructure assessment and runtime behaviour. | The Cloud Security Alliance’s Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide sets out twelve threat categories for agents, from control hijacking and memory manipulation to untraceable actions. | MITRE ATLAS catalogues adversary tactics and techniques against AI, with real case studies, and gives findings a common language. | NIST’s adversarial machine learning taxonomy defines attack types and mitigations for predictive and generative AI. | A simple threat ontology, used by Microsoft’s red team, records each finding as a system, an actor, tactics and techniques, a weakness and an impact. | And purple teaming brings attackers and defenders together, so every attack also tests detection and response.

Combine human creativity with automated scale
Structure the work with OWASP, CSA, MITRE ATLAS and NIST
Purple team, so attacks also test detection
scenes.say: To recap. | Run red teaming as a cycle: plan, map, attack, assess, report, then fix and retest. | Combine human creativity with automated scale. | Structure the work with the OWASP and CSA guides, MITRE ATLAS and NIST’s taxonomy. | And purple team, so that every attack also tests detection and response.

blocks.md:
### What makes AI red teaming different
- **Probabilistic results:** the same attack can succeed or fail on different attempts, so findings carry success rates (Section 2).
- **Beyond security:** AI red teams also look for safety and responsible AI harms, such as dangerous advice, bias or privacy leaks, which ordinary users can trigger by accident.
- **Adversarial and benign personas:** test as a skilled attacker, an opportunistic user, an insider, a compromised data source or tool, and a well-meaning user who stumbles into harm.
- **Simple attacks work:** Microsoft’s red team found that cheap, manual techniques often beat sophisticated mathematical ones, so test the whole system, not just the model’s robustness.
- **Never finished:** mitigations reduce risk but don’t eliminate it. The aim is to raise attackers’ costs through repeated break-fix cycles.

### Methodologies and frameworks
| Framework | What it offers |
|---|---|
| **OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide** (January 2025) | A blueprint covering model evaluation, implementation testing, infrastructure assessment and runtime behaviour analysis |
| **CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide** (2025, with the OWASP AI Exchange) | Twelve threat categories for agents: authorisation and control hijacking; checker-out-of-the-loop; critical system interaction; goal and instruction manipulation; hallucination exploitation; impact chain and blast radius; knowledge base poisoning; memory and context manipulation; orchestration and multi-agent exploitation; resource and service exhaustion; supply chain and dependency attacks; and untraceability |
| **MITRE ATLAS** | Adversary tactics, techniques and case studies for AI systems, used to plan scenarios and to map findings (Module 6.5) |
| **NIST AI 100-2** (2025 edition) | A taxonomy and terminology of adversarial machine learning attacks and mitigations, for predictive and generative AI |
| **Microsoft’s threat ontology** | Each finding recorded as a system, an actor, tactics, techniques and procedures, a weakness and an impact |

### Regulatory drivers
- **EU AI Act:** providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must perform and document adversarial testing (**Article 55**), and the **General-Purpose AI Code of Practice** (July 2025) describes how in its safety and security chapter. High-risk systems must achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cyber security (**Article 15**), confirmed through testing.
- **NIST AI 600-1**, the generative AI profile of the AI RMF, recommends red teaming as part of managing generative AI risk, and many national AI safety and security institutes publish red teaming guidance.

### Running an AI red team
- **Team:** security testers, ML engineers, subject experts (such as clinicians or lawyers, for domain harms), and people with different languages and cultural knowledge. Provide wellbeing support for anyone reviewing harmful content.
- **Order of work:** manual exploration first, to understand behaviour and find promising weaknesses; then automation, to scale variants and measure rates (Section 4).
- **Logging:** record every prompt, response, tool call, setting and version, so findings can be reproduced (Module 6.5).
- **Purple teaming:** share findings with defenders as they happen, so detections and guardrails improve during the engagement, not months later.
- **External testing:** bug bounty programmes and independent red teams add diversity and independence once internal testing is mature.

blocks.title: Red teaming terms
cards: Repeated rounds of testing, mitigation and retesting that raise an attacker’s costs over time.
A tester acting as an ordinary user, to find harms people can trigger by accident.
Attackers and defenders working together, so each attack also tests detection and response.
A structure for recording findings: system, actor, tactics and techniques, weakness and impact.
A CSA agentic threat category: the agent acts without the human or automated check that should review it.

blocks.title: The red team that only ran a tool
blocks.md: An organisation’s red team runs an automated tool against a new HR agent and reports a 0.4% attack success rate across 5,000 generated prompts, recommending launch. Nobody explored the agent manually, and the tool’s test library predates the agent’s new ability to update payroll records.

q.q: What is the MAIN weakness in this assessment?
o: The sample of 5,000 prompts was far too small to give a meaningful success rate
No human explored new capabilities, such as payroll updates, that the tool wasn’t built for
Automated tools should never be used for red teaming, because their results can’t be trusted
The attack success rate should have been reported as a fraction, not as a percentage
q.why: Automation measures known techniques at scale, but misses novel, contextual risks such as a new payroll capability. Human-led exploration of new features, followed by automation of what it finds, is the effective combination.

blocks.title: Red teaming questions
blocks.md: Look for **objective-led**, **system-level** testing run as a **break-fix cycle**, with **manual exploration before automation**, **diverse personas** (including benign users), findings mapped to **MITRE ATLAS** or OWASP categories, and **purple teaming** so that detection improves too. A single automated scan is not a red team.

q.q: Which practice BEST describes purple teaming in an AI red team engagement?
o: Testing only at weekends, so that the defending team is unaware of the activity
Sharing attacks with defenders as they happen, so that detection improves too
Assigning the same person to build the guardrails and then to attack them
Publishing all successful attacks online, so other organisations can learn
q.why: Purple teaming pairs attackers and defenders, so each attack also tests and improves detection and response during the engagement.

scenes.title: Using AI to test AI
scenes.sub: AI-assisted tools for evaluating controls and finding attack paths
scenes.say: Human red teamers can try hundreds of ideas. Attacker models can try millions of variations, and AI agents are now finding real vulnerabilities in software. Used well, AI-assisted tools extend coverage dramatically. Used carelessly, they create false confidence. | This video covers AI-assisted security tools for evaluating AI controls and discovering novel attack paths.

scenes.title: An automated red-teaming loop
scenes.say: Here is the core loop of automated red teaming. It starts with seed objectives from the threat model, such as revealing a canary record. | An attacker model generates test inputs for each objective, and mutates them: rephrasing, splitting across turns, or changing format and language. | The inputs go to the target system, in staging, with canary data. | A scorer judges each response. It might be a classifier, or another model acting as a judge. | The verdict feeds back to the attacker, which refines its next attempts, so the search concentrates on weak spots. | People review samples and every claimed success, because judges make mistakes. | And confirmed attacks join a regression suite that runs on every release, so fixed weaknesses stay fixed.

scenes.title: AI-assisted testing tools

items.d: Agents that find flaws in code

scenes.say: A growing set of tools puts AI to work on testing. | PyRIT, Microsoft’s open-source risk identification toolkit, orchestrates attacker models, input conversions and scorers. | garak, from NVIDIA, runs probes that check language models for known weaknesses, with detectors that judge the results. | promptfoo generates adversarial test cases through red-team plugins, and runs evaluations in continuous integration. | Inspect, from the UK’s AI Security Institute, is a framework for building and running evaluations. | The Adversarial Robustness Toolbox covers classic machine learning attacks: evasion, poisoning, extraction and inference. | And AI vulnerability hunters, such as Google’s Big Sleep, use agents to find flaws in the software around AI.

scenes.title: AI finds real vulnerabilities

events.d: AI agent finds a memory-safety flaw in SQLite
An AI pentester tops a US leaderboard
A flaw found before planned exploitation
54 of 63 planted flaws found; 18 real ones

scenes.say: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has moved quickly from research to results. | In October 2024, Google’s Big Sleep agent found a memory-safety flaw in the widely used SQLite database engine. | By mid-2025, an autonomous penetration-testing system, XBOW, had topped HackerOne’s US bug bounty leaderboard. | In July 2025, Big Sleep found another SQLite flaw that, according to Google, threat actors were preparing to exploit, so it was fixed first. | And in August 2025, at the finals of DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge, AI systems found fifty-four of sixty-three planted vulnerabilities, patched forty-three, and discovered eighteen real ones. The same techniques can be pointed at your own AI stack.

scenes.title: Using AI testers safely

items.d: Hard limits on targets and actions

scenes.say: AI testers need controls of their own. | Keep them in scope. Autonomous testing agents need hard technical limits on targets, rates and actions, not just instructions. | Calibrate the judges. Check automated scorers against human-labelled samples, because a lenient judge hides failures, and a strict one floods you with false alarms. | Protect test data. Adversarial inputs and harmful outputs shouldn’t be sent to unapproved services. | Expect counter-injection. The system under test can manipulate the attacker or the judge, just as it might manipulate any other model. | Record model versions, settings and random seeds, so results can be reproduced. | And confirm before reporting: a person verifies every finding.

items: Automate the loop: attacker, target, scorer, human review
Use tools such as PyRIT, garak, promptfoo, Inspect and ART
AI can find novel attack paths and real vulnerabilities
Scope, calibrate, protect data, and verify findings
scenes.say: To recap. | Automated red teaming loops through an attacker model, the target, a scorer and human review. | Tools such as PyRIT, garak, promptfoo, Inspect and the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox make this practical. | AI can find novel attack paths and real vulnerabilities, at a scale people can’t match. | But keep AI testers in scope, calibrate their judges, protect test data, and verify every finding.

blocks.md:
### What AI-assisted tools do
| Capability | How it works | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Automated red teaming** | Attacker models generate and mutate adversarial inputs; scorers judge responses; results feed back to refine attacks | PyRIT; promptfoo red-team plugins; research methods such as PAIR and TAP |
| **Probe libraries** | Large collections of known attack patterns run against a model or application, with detectors scoring the outputs | garak |
| **Evaluation frameworks** | Reusable tasks, datasets and scorers for repeatable evaluations of capabilities and safeguards | Inspect; promptfoo |
| **Classic adversarial ML** | Evasion, poisoning, extraction and inference attacks against predictive models | Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART); TextAttack |
| **LLM judges** | A model scores outputs against a rubric, at scale (Module 1.3) | Built into most frameworks |
| **AI vulnerability discovery** | Agents that read code, fuzz and reason about flaws in the software stack | Google Big Sleep; the DARPA AI Cyber Challenge systems, released as open source |

### Evaluating AI controls
Use these tools to measure whether controls work, not just whether a model misbehaves:
- **Guardrails and classifiers:** run labelled sets of adversarial and benign inputs, and measure **detection rates and false positive rates** for each category (Module 4.4).
- **Access and agency controls:** check that tool scopes, approval steps and retrieval permissions hold under adversarial pressure.
- **Monitoring:** confirm that attacks raise the alerts they should (Module 5.3).
- **Regression:** turn every confirmed finding into an automated test that runs on each release, so fixes stay fixed (Module 6.6).

### Finding novel attack paths
- **Permission analysis:** map which agents can read untrusted content, reach private data and communicate externally. Simon Willison called the combination of all three the **lethal trifecta** (2025), because it lets injected instructions steal data. Automated analysis can flag these combinations before an attacker finds them.
- **Multi-step exploration:** agentic testers chain tools and steps the way an attacker would, revealing paths that single-prompt tests miss.
- **Variant generation:** once a person finds a weakness, attacker models generate thousands of variants to show how general it is.

### Cautions
- **False confidence:** a test library only finds what it was built to find; new capabilities need human exploration (Section 3).
- **Judge reliability:** LLM judges can be lenient, strict, biased or manipulated. Calibrate them against human labels, and review samples.
- **Scope and safety:** autonomous testers need technical limits on targets, rates and actions, and a kill switch.
- **Data handling:** adversarial inputs and harmful outputs are sensitive, so keep them in approved tools and storage.
- **Dual use:** attackers use the same tools. Control access to them, and log their use.

blocks.title: The generous judge
blocks.md: A bank’s automated red-teaming pipeline uses a language model as a judge. It reports a 0.2% attack success rate for tests that try to make the assistant give prohibited investment advice. A security engineer manually reviews 200 responses the judge marked as safe, and finds 14 that give the prohibited advice.

q.q: What should the team do FIRST?
o: Accept the 0.2% figure, since automated judges are more consistent than human reviewers
Recalibrate the judge against human-labelled samples, then re-score the test results
Replace the judge with simple keyword matching, which can’t make the same mistakes
Stop testing for prohibited advice, since the results are clearly too unreliable to use
q.why: The manual sample shows the judge is missing real failures: 14 of 200 is 7%. Calibrating the judge against human labels and re-scoring restores trust in the numbers. Accepting the figure ignores the evidence, keyword matching has its own blind spots, and stopping testing removes visibility.

blocks.title: AI-assisted testing questions
blocks.md: AI-assisted tools **extend coverage and repeatability**; they don’t replace human judgement. Expect the best answers to **calibrate automated judges**, keep autonomous testers **technically in scope**, **protect test data**, **verify findings** before reporting, and turn confirmed attacks into **regression tests**. For agents, look for permission combinations such as the **lethal trifecta**.

q.q: An organisation is reviewing its AI agents for exposure to injected instructions. Which combination of capabilities in a single agent is MOST dangerous?
o: Reading internal documentation, and summarising it for staff in a chat window
Reading untrusted content, accessing private data and communicating externally
Generating images for the marketing team, and saving them to a shared drive
Answering questions about public products from a curated knowledge base
q.why: Untrusted content can carry instructions, private data gives them something to steal, and external communication provides a way out. Together they form the "lethal trifecta"; removing any one of them breaks the path.

sections.title: Deep dive: jailbreak and injection families

scenes.title: Why jailbreaks work
scenes.sub: Attack families, their mechanisms and how to test for them
scenes.say: Section two listed jailbreak families as something to test. This deep dive explains why they work, how each family operates at a high level, and how to measure a system’s resistance. | As always in this course, it stays conceptual: the aim is to recognise and test these patterns, not to reproduce them.

scenes.title: Two root causes
rows: Safety data as broad as ability
scenes.say: Research by Wei and colleagues in 2023 traced jailbreaks to two root causes. | The first is competing objectives: the model’s drive to be helpful and follow instructions is set against its safety training. The second is mismatched generalisation: the model’s abilities reach inputs that its safety training never covered. | Role-play frames, and instructions to begin with an affirmative reply, exploit competing objectives. Encodings, ciphers and low-resource languages exploit mismatched generalisation. | Defences follow from the causes: safety training on these conflicts, safety data as broad as the model’s abilities, and independent classifiers that don’t share the model’s blind spots.

scenes.title: Families to cover in a test plan

items.d: A fictional frame seems to permit it
Hundreds of fake dialogues in one prompt

scenes.say: A test plan should cover at least eight families. | Role-play and personas wrap a request in a fictional or hypothetical frame that seems to permit it. | Obfuscation and encoding hide the request in a format that filters and safety training handle poorly. | Low-resource languages exploit the fact that most safety data is in English. | Many-shot attacks fill a long context window with hundreds of fabricated dialogues in which an assistant complies, and success rises steadily with their number. | Multi-turn escalation moves in small steps, each harmless on its own. | Optimised suffixes are strings found by an algorithm rather than a person, and they can transfer between models. | Payload splitting asks the model to combine fragments that are harmless separately. | And multimodal attacks carry instructions in images, documents or audio. Indirect prompt injection uses all of these tricks, delivered through content the system reads.

scenes.title: Multi-turn escalation, in outline

msgs.t: [Turn 1: a harmless question about the topic’s history]
[Turns 2–4: each asks for a little more, building on the last answer]
[Each reply goes slightly further than the one before]
Result: the final reply crosses the policy line. Asked directly, the same request was refused.

notes.d: Nothing in the first turn would trip a filter.
The model’s own answers become the foundation.
Each request is only slightly beyond the last.
No single turn looks clearly harmful.
Score and monitor conversations, not single turns.

scenes.say: Here is the outline of a multi-turn escalation, the pattern Microsoft researchers named Crescendo in 2024. It begins with a harmless question about a topic’s history or background. | The model gives a general, factual overview. Nothing so far would trip a filter. | Over the next few turns, each request asks for a little more, often building on the model’s own previous answer. | Because each reply goes only slightly further than the last, no single turn looks clearly harmful, and the model tends to stay consistent with what it has already said. | Eventually the conversation reaches content the model would have refused if asked directly. That is why tests, monitoring and classifiers must judge whole conversations, not single prompts.

scenes.title: Optimised suffixes and transfer
scenes.say: The greedy coordinate gradient attack, or GCG, published by Zou and colleagues in 2023, starts with a request that open-weight models refuse. | Using the models’ gradients, it searches token by token for a suffix that makes an affirmative reply more likely, keeping the best swap at each step. | The result is a string that looks like gibberish to people, but reliably changes the models’ behaviour. | Suffixes optimised against several open models often transferred to closed commercial models, which the attacker never had gradients for. Open models can be stepping stones to closed ones. | Defences include perplexity filters, which flag unnatural text, input and output classifiers, and adversarial training. But attacks can be optimised to read naturally too, so no single filter is enough.

items: Jailbreaks exploit competing objectives or gaps in safety training
Test every family, in every language and input channel
Suffixes found on open models can transfer to closed ones
Report success rates alongside false refusals
scenes.say: To recap. | Jailbreaks exploit competing objectives, or gaps between a model’s abilities and its safety training. | A test plan covers every family, in every language and input channel the system supports, including whole conversations. | Attacks optimised on open models can transfer to closed ones, so a hosted model isn’t safe just because its weights are secret. | And results are reported as success rates over repeated trials, alongside the false refusals any defence causes.

blocks.md:
### Why safety training fails
Wei, Haghtalab and Steinhardt (2023) traced jailbreaks to two failure modes. With **competing objectives**, the model’s drive to be helpful and follow instructions is set against its safety training, for example by role-play frames or instructions to begin with an affirmative reply. With **mismatched generalisation**, the model’s abilities extend to inputs its safety training never covered, such as encodings, ciphers or low-resource languages. Defences follow from this: safety training as broad as the model’s abilities, plus independent classifiers that don’t share its blind spots.

### Families to cover in a test plan
| Family | How it works | What to test | Typical defences |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Role-play and personas** | A fictional or hypothetical frame seems to permit the request | Persona and scenario variants | Safety training on framed requests; output classifiers |
| **Obfuscation and encoding** | The request is hidden in an encoding, cipher or unusual format | Encoded and transformed variants | Normalise or decode inputs; classify outputs |
| **Low-resource languages** | Translation sidesteps mostly English safety data (Yong et al., 2023) | The same tests in several languages | Multilingual safety data and classifiers |
| **Many-shot** | Hundreds of fabricated dialogues in one long prompt (Anil et al., 2024) | Long-context variants | Prompt classification and modification |
| **Multi-turn escalation** | Gradual steps, each harmless alone, as in Crescendo (Russinovich et al., 2024) | Whole conversations | Conversation-level classifiers and monitoring |
| **Optimised suffixes** | Machine-found strings, as in GCG (Zou et al., 2023) | Automated attack tools | Perplexity filters; classifiers; adversarial training |
| **Payload splitting** | Harmless fragments the model is asked to combine | Split and recombined requests | Output classifiers; intent checks |
| **Multimodal** | Instructions carried in images, documents or audio | Every input channel | Classify extracted text and media |

**Indirect prompt injection** (Greshake et al., 2023) uses the same tricks, delivered through content the system reads, such as web pages, emails and retrieved documents. Tests must plant them in each data source and tool result (Section 2).

### Automated and optimised attacks
- **GCG** (Zou et al., 2023) uses gradients from open-weight models to find a suffix that makes an affirmative reply more likely. Suffixes optimised against several open models transferred to closed commercial models.
- **PAIR** and **TAP** use an attacker model to refine readable jailbreaks, often within a few dozen queries (Section 4).
- **Best-of-N** (Hughes et al., 2024) samples many random variations of a request, such as changes to capitalisation, until one succeeds. Success keeps rising with the number of attempts, so rate limits and monitoring matter.
- **Many-shot** success rises with the number of examples, following a power law. In Anthropic’s study, limiting context length would stop it but sacrifices value, fine-tuning only delayed it, and classifying and modifying prompts before they reached the model cut one attack’s success from 61% to 2%.

### Measuring results
Report the **attack success rate** for each family over repeated trials, because outputs are probabilistic, and pair it with the **false refusal rate** on benign requests, so that a fix that blocks legitimate use is visible. Public benchmarks include **HarmBench** and **JailbreakBench** for jailbreaks and **AgentDojo** for injection against agents. Map findings to **OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection** and to **MITRE ATLAS** techniques **AML.T0051** (LLM Prompt Injection) and **AML.T0054** (LLM Jailbreak).

blocks.title: Testing jailbreak resistance
items: Choose the families
Cover every family in the table, in each language and input channel the system supports, including indirect channels.
Define success
Agree what counts as a successful attack for this system, with a scoring rubric and worked examples.
Repeat the trials
Run each test many times and report success rates, because outputs vary from run to run.
Measure the cost
Run a benign set alongside, to measure the false refusals that defences cause.
Retest and track
Add successful attacks to the regression suite and track rates release by release (Module 6.6).

q.q: A researcher used an open-weight model to optimise an adversarial suffix. The team’s application runs on a closed, hosted model from a different provider. What is the MOST accurate assessment?
o: The risk is negligible, since nobody can compute the hosted model’s gradients
The suffix may still transfer, so the application should be tested against it
The provider’s terms of use forbid such attacks, so testing isn’t needed
Only models sharing the same architecture and weights could be affected
q.why: Optimised suffixes have transferred from open models to closed commercial ones, so secret weights don’t make the attack irrelevant. Terms of use don’t stop attackers, and transfer doesn’t require identical architectures or weights.

quiz.q: Why should an AI security assessment scope the whole system rather than just the model?
o: Models can’t be tested directly, so only the surrounding system can be assessed
Many serious failures happen where components meet, such as retrieval and tools
Regulators prohibit testing models that were developed by a third-party provider
The model is always the most secure component, so testing it adds little value
quiz.why: Real failures often occur at the joins: retrieved content reaching tools, outputs reaching downstream systems, or approvals that can be bypassed.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of rules of engagement in an AI red team exercise?
o: To list the attacks testers must avoid mentioning on social media afterwards
To set the authority, scope, limits and stop rules before testing starts
To guarantee that the system will pass the test without any findings at all
To describe the product’s features for the marketing team’s launch plan
quiz.why: Signed rules of engagement make testing authorised, bounded and safe, with clear stop rules and reporting.

quiz.q: What does grey box testing mean in an AI assessment?
o: Testers start with no information at all about the system that they are testing
Testers get some internal knowledge, such as the architecture and system prompts
Testers get full access to code, weights and training data from the very start
Testers may only use automated tools, and never any manual testing techniques
quiz.why: Grey box testing shares partial knowledge, so testers spend their time finding weaknesses rather than guessing how the system works.

quiz.q: What is a canary tool in an indirect injection test?
o: A tool that blocks every instruction found inside the retrieved documents
A harmless tool that records it was called, proving an instruction was obeyed
A tool that alerts users whenever an agent is about to transfer any money
A monitoring tool that measures the agent’s response time under heavy load
quiz.why: A canary tool has no real effect; its only job is to show that the agent followed an instruction planted in data.

quiz.q: Which test is specific to retrieval-augmented generation?
o: Checking that the chatbot’s login page enforces multi-factor authentication
Checking whether retrieval returns documents the user isn’t permitted to see
Checking that the model’s weights are encrypted when they are stored at rest
Checking that the GPU cluster’s drivers are patched to the latest version
quiz.why: Permission-aware retrieval is a RAG-specific control: retrieval must enforce the requesting user’s document permissions.

quiz.q: Why are AI security test results reported as attack success rates?
o: Rates are required by every AI regulation for all types of AI system
Outputs vary between attempts, so a rate shows how often attacks work
Rates are easier to present to executives than a list of findings
Most automated testing tools can’t record the result of a single test
quiz.why: Because AI systems are stochastic, the same attack can succeed on some attempts and fail on others; a rate over many attempts captures that.

quiz.q: Which agentic test checks whether an injected instruction can affect later sessions?
o: A runaway loop test that counts how many tool calls the agent makes
A memory persistence test, across later sessions and other users
A permission-aware retrieval test run against the document index
A load test that measures the agent’s latency during peak traffic
quiz.why: Memory persistence tests check whether planted instructions survive in an agent’s memory and influence future sessions.

quiz.q: Which stage of the AI red team cycle follows reporting?
o: Planning next year’s budget for the whole security team
Fixing the weaknesses that were found, and then retesting
Deleting all test logs to protect the testers’ privacy
Publishing the findings openly on the company website
quiz.why: Red teaming is a break-fix cycle: builders mitigate, and the red team retests to confirm the fixes.

quiz.q: What does the CSA Agentic AI Red Teaming Guide provide?
o: A certification scheme for organisations that develop agentic AI products
Twelve threat categories for red teaming agents, such as memory manipulation
A list of approved AI agent vendors for government procurement in the EU
A legal template for contracts between agent developers and customers
quiz.why: The 2025 guide, developed with the OWASP AI Exchange, sets out twelve agentic threat categories with test approaches.

quiz.q: Why do AI red teams emulate benign users as well as attackers?
o: Benign users are easier to emulate, which keeps testing costs to a minimum
Ordinary users can trigger harms by accident, which matter as much as attacks
Regulations require at least half of all red team personas to be benign users
Attackers always pretend to be benign users, so the two personas are identical
quiz.why: Many AI harms, such as dangerous advice or privacy leaks, arise from ordinary use, so red teams test benign personas too.

quiz.q: What role does the scorer play in automated red teaming?
o: It generates new adversarial inputs from the seed objectives
It judges whether each response shows a successful attack
It deploys the target system into the staging environment
It writes the final report for non-technical stakeholders
quiz.why: A scorer, such as a classifier or an LLM judge, decides whether each response counts as a success, and its verdicts feed back to the attacker.

quiz.q: Why must LLM judges be calibrated against human labels?
o: LLM judges can only score responses that are written in English
They can be lenient, strict or manipulated, distorting the results
Human labels are needed before any model can legally be deployed
Calibration makes the judge run faster on very large test sets
quiz.why: Uncalibrated judges can hide failures or raise false alarms, and the system under test may even manipulate them.

quiz.q: What is the "lethal trifecta" for AI agents?
o: Three agents working together, so no single agent can be compromised
Untrusted content, access to private data and external communication
Three failed sign-in attempts, after which an agent’s account is locked
Training, fine-tuning and deployment, all done in a single environment
quiz.why: An agent with all three can be steered by injected instructions into stealing data; removing any one breaks the path.

quiz.q: A model refuses a harmful request in English but answers the same request translated into a low-resource language. Which root cause does this illustrate?
o: Competing objectives: helpfulness overrides safety training
Mismatched generalisation: ability outreaches safety training
Context overflow: the system prompt was truncated in translation
Model drift: the provider updated the model between the two tests
quiz.why: The model can understand the language, but its safety training didn’t cover it well, so its abilities generalise further than its safety behaviour. That is mismatched generalisation.

quiz.q: Many-shot jailbreaking depends MOST on which model feature?
o: Access to the model’s gradients through an open-weight release
A long context window that can hold hundreds of examples
Tool use that lets the model fetch content from the web
A high sampling temperature that makes outputs more random
quiz.why: The attack packs hundreds of fabricated dialogues into one prompt, which only fits in a long context window. Its success rises with the number of examples.

quiz.q: A team’s jailbreak tests show a 2% attack success rate after a new classifier is added, down from 30%. What else must the report include for a fair view of the change?
o: The names of the testers who ran each of the attack families
How often benign requests are wrongly refused, before and after
The model’s accuracy on general knowledge benchmarks only
The exact prompts used, published for the whole company to see
quiz.why: A defence that blocks attacks by also blocking legitimate requests can look excellent on attack success alone. Pairing attack success with false refusals shows the real trade-off.

quiz.q: An attacker submits thousands of slightly varied versions of a refused request, changing capitalisation and spacing, until one succeeds. Which control MOST directly counters this approach?
o: A longer system prompt that restates the safety policy in detail
Rate limits, and monitoring for bursts of near-identical requests
Lowering the sampling temperature for every request to zero
Translating every request into English before it reaches the model
quiz.why: Best-of-N attacks rely on volume: success keeps rising with the number of attempts. Rate limits and monitoring cap the attempts and reveal the pattern. Varied inputs still produce varied outputs at a temperature of 0.

exam.q: A bank plans an assessment of a customer chatbot that uses RAG and can open support tickets. The project manager proposes testing only the underlying model with a public jailbreak benchmark. What is the BEST response?
o: Agree, because the model is where all of the chatbot’s security weaknesses originate
Scope the whole system, including retrieval, ticket actions, guardrails and monitoring
Agree, provided the benchmark is run twice, to allow for the model’s randomness
Replace the assessment with a review of the model vendor’s SOC 2 report instead
exam.why: Benchmarks of the model miss system-level risks such as retrieval permissions, injection through documents and ticket actions. Scope the whole system, with scenarios drawn from its threat model.

exam.q: During a red team exercise, a tester sees what appears to be real customer data in the staging assistant’s responses. The rules of engagement include a stop rule for this case. What should the tester do FIRST?
o: Continue testing to find out how much real data can be extracted, then report it
Stop testing at once and notify the engagement lead, as the stop rule requires
Delete the responses from the logs so that the real data isn’t retained
Post the finding in the team’s open chat channel to warn colleagues quickly
exam.why: Stop rules exist for exactly this situation: halt, escalate and let the lead manage the potential data exposure. Continuing, deleting evidence or broadcasting the finding are all inappropriate.

exam.q: Which success criterion is BEST for a red team test of a support agent’s refund tool?
o: The agent should generally behave securely and responsibly in most situations
Unauthorised refunds succeed in under 0.5% of 500 attempts per technique class
The testers should feel satisfied that they tried their hardest to break the agent
The agent must never produce any output that the testers find surprising
exam.why: A good criterion is measurable and agreed in advance, accounting for repeated attempts. Vague or subjective criteria can’t support a decision.

exam.q: A legal research assistant retrieves from a shared index. Testers find that a junior employee’s question returned a confidential board memo. Which control failure does this MOST likely indicate?
o: The model wasn’t fine-tuned on enough legal documents during its development
Retrieval isn’t enforcing the requesting user’s document permissions
The assistant’s guardrails were set too strictly for the legal domain
The index was too large for the embedding model to handle accurately
exam.why: Returning documents a user isn’t entitled to see is a failure of permission-aware retrieval, not of model quality or guardrail strictness.

exam.q: Testers want to show that an email agent can be steered by instructions hidden in incoming messages, without risking harm. Which approach is BEST?
o: Send real phishing emails to staff, and see whether the agent forwards them on
Plant a test email that asks the agent to call a monitored canary tool
Ask the agent directly whether it would follow instructions found in emails
Review only the agent’s code, since its behaviour can’t be tested
exam.why: A canary proves the weakness safely and observably. Real phishing harms people, asking the agent proves nothing, and code review alone can’t show model behaviour.

exam.q: An agent passed every single-prompt injection test, but a red teamer succeeded by spreading an attack across six conversation turns. What does this show about the test design?
o: Single-prompt tests are sufficient, so the red teamer’s result can be ignored
The test suite needs multi-turn cases, since attacks can build up gradually
Conversations longer than five turns should be blocked for every user
The red teamer should have kept to the existing single-prompt test cases
exam.why: Multi-turn attacks escalate gradually and evade single-prompt safeguards, so suites must include them. Blocking long conversations is disproportionate.

exam.q: An organisation wants to start red teaming a new agent with novel capabilities. Which approach is MOST effective?
o: Run an automated tool’s default test library only, since it covers known attacks
Explore manually first, then automate variants and regressions of what is found
Wait until a public benchmark covers the agent’s capabilities before testing
Ask the developers to red team their own agent, since they know it best
exam.why: Human exploration finds novel, contextual weaknesses in new capabilities; automation then scales and preserves them. Default libraries, waiting and self-testing all leave gaps.

exam.q: A red team shows that an agent can be manipulated into exfiltrating data, but the SOC saw no alerts during the whole exercise. Which practice would have MOST improved the outcome?
o: Running the exercise without telling anyone, to keep it as realistic as possible
Purple teaming, so that defenders tune detections during the engagement
Reducing the number of attacks, so that the SOC isn’t overwhelmed by alerts
Repeating the same exercise next year, with exactly the same test cases
exam.why: Purple teaming turns each attack into a detection test, so monitoring gaps are found and fixed during the engagement.

exam.q: A team’s autonomous testing agent began probing a third-party API that was out of scope, after following a link in a response. Which control was MISSING?
o: A larger compute budget for the testing agent, so that it could finish sooner
Technical scope limits on targets and actions, enforced outside the agent
A better system prompt asking the agent politely to stay within its scope
A faster model, so the agent spends less time on each individual target
exam.why: Autonomous testers can be steered like any agent, so scope must be enforced technically, outside the model, for example with network allow-lists.

exam.q: An automated pipeline reports that a new guardrail blocks 99% of adversarial prompts. What should ALSO be measured before relying on it?
o: How long the guardrail’s vendor has been in business
The false positive rate on benign requests, by category
How many engineers reviewed the guardrail configuration
Whether the guardrail was bought or developed in-house
exam.why: A guardrail that blocks attacks but also blocks many legitimate requests may be unusable; results by category also reveal weak spots hidden in the average.

exam.q: A red team lead is planning jailbreak testing for a multilingual customer assistant that accepts text, images and file uploads. Which test plan is BEST?
o: Run the public HarmBench suite in English and report its overall score
Cover each attack family in every supported language and input channel
Test text prompts thoroughly, since images and files are lower risk
Focus on optimised suffixes, as they are the most advanced technique
exam.why: Jailbreaks exploit gaps in safety training, which are often language-specific and channel-specific. A public benchmark in one language, or one family alone, leaves those gaps untested.

exam.q: After a perplexity filter is deployed, a red team finds that machine-optimised jailbreak strings are blocked, but readable jailbreaks written by an attacker model still succeed. What is the BEST next step?
o: Lower the perplexity threshold until the readable attacks are blocked too
Add complementary defences, such as classifiers on inputs and outputs
Close the finding, since automated suffix attacks were the main threat
Ban attacker models from being used in future red team exercises
exam.why: Perplexity filters catch unnatural text, not fluent attacks. Pushing the threshold far enough to block fluent text would block normal users too, so layered classifiers and other controls are needed.

exam.q: A bank’s red team reports that a jailbreak succeeded in 4 of 100 attempts. The product owner wants it marked as not reproducible because it failed when re-run once. What is the BEST response?
o: Mark it not reproducible, since it failed when it was re-run
Report it as a 4% success rate, since outputs are probabilistic
Discard it, since anything below 5% is within normal tolerance
Retest at a temperature of 0 and report only the single result
exam.why: Model outputs vary between runs, so a single failed retry proves nothing. Findings are reported as rates over repeated trials, then judged against the system’s risk tolerance.
